title: Smooth multiplicative cover lifting a projective representation
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes and their homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme]. All algebraic groups in this statement are affine and of finite type over $F$ [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Smoothness and connectedness are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Let $G$ be smooth connected. For a nonzero finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $V$, $\mathbf P(V)$ is the scheme of one-dimensional quotients of $V$, with tautological quotient line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P(V)}(1)$; $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is the group scheme $A\mapsto\operatorname{Aut}_A(V\otimes_F A)$, $\operatorname{SL}(V)$ is its determinant-one subgroup, and $\operatorname{PGL}(V)$ is the fppf sheaf quotient of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ by its scalar subgroup $\mathbf G_m$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Given a group-scheme homomorphism $a:G\to\operatorname{PGL}(V)$, form the group-scheme fibre product $E=G\times_{\operatorname{PGL}(V)}\operatorname{SL}(V)$ and let $H=(E_{\mathrm{red}})^\circ$ be the identity component of its reduced closed subscheme (reduced means nilpotents are removed, and the identity component is the connected component containing the identity). The group law of $E$ restricts to $H$, and $H$ is smooth connected. Its projection $q:H\to G$ is a multiplicative isogeny. A multiplicative isogeny $q:H\to G$ means a group-scheme homomorphism for which $F[G]\to F[H]$ is faithfully flat (extension of scalars is exact and detects zero modules), and whose scheme-theoretic kernel is $D(M)=\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ for a finite abelian group $M$. The group algebra has basis $e^m$, multiplication $e^me^n=e^{m+n}$, comultiplication $e^m\mapsto e^m\otimes e^m$, counit $e^m\mapsto1$ and antipode $e^m\mapsto e^{-m}$. The second projection restricts to a homomorphism $\rho:H\to\operatorname{SL}(V)$ with $\overline\rho=a\circ q$ in $\operatorname{PGL}(V)$. Scheme-theoretically, $\ker q$ is a closed subgroup of the scalar group $\mu_n=\operatorname{Spec}F[z,z^{-1}]/(z^n-1)$, $n=\dim_F V\geq1$. No prime-to-characteristic assumption on $n$ is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 18.22, proof, printed p.393 (pullback of SL(V) to G); Example 5.49, printed p.111 (SL_n to PGL_n has kernel mu_n); Propositions 1.26 and 1.38, Corollary 1.39, printed pp.13,17; the reduced identity-component reduction explicitly used in Proposition 18.6(a), printed p.388; Proposition 5.47, printed pp.110--111.

proof.text: First dispose of $n=1$. In a basis of $V$, $\operatorname{GL}(V)=\mathbf G_m$, its scalar quotient $\operatorname{PGL}(V)$ is trivial, and determinant is the identity on $\mathbf G_m$, so $\operatorname{SL}(V)=1$. The fibre-product universal property [def-pc-fibre-product] gives $E=G$. Since $G$ is smooth, it is reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], and since it is connected its identity component is itself. Thus $H=G$ and $q=\mathrm{id}_G$. This coordinate map is faithfully flat, its kernel is $1=D(0)=\mu_1$, and the unique map $\rho:G\to1$ has the required projectivization. Henceforth $n\geq2$.

source.place: Example 5.49, printed p.111, rank-one specialization; Proposition 1.26, printed p.13

proof.text: Choose a basis $V\simeq F^n$. The matrix groups are the groups of [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover]. Its quotient agrees with the fppf quotient in the item: [lem-sfb-projective-frames-pgl] identifies the same determinant-open projective matrix scheme as the Zariski quotient by scalars, so matrices lift Zariski locally and their equality is exactly scalar equality; these also give the universal quotient sheaf for fppf coverings. Write $s:\operatorname{SL}_n\to\operatorname{PGL}_n$. The central-cover node gives that $s$ is finite and surjective, with scalar kernel $\mu_n$. By [def-pc-fibre-product] the fibre product $E$ exists; multiplication and inverse are componentwise on pairs $(g,u)$ with $a(g)=s(u)$, since $a,s$ are homomorphisms. Their identities follow after either projection by uniqueness in that universal property. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $E$ is affine. Its projection $p:E\to G$ is finite by [lem-trf-finite-radicial-basechange] and surjective by [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change]. It is of finite type: on affines a finite module algebra is generated as an algebra by any finite set of module generators. Combining these generators with generators of $F[G]$ shows that $E$ is of finite type over $F$.

source.place: Proposition 18.22, proof, printed p.393; Example 5.49, printed p.111; finite and surjective base change: Stacks 01WL and 01S1

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component] to $E$ over the algebraically closed field $F$. It gives the open and closed subgroup $E^\circ$ and its smooth connected reduced subgroup $(E^\circ)_{\mathrm{red}}$. Reduction does not change underlying spaces and restricts on an open by quotienting its affine rings by their nilradicals [def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction]. Therefore $(E^\circ)_{\mathrm{red}}=(E_{\mathrm{red}})^\circ=H$ as closed subschemes of $E$: both are the reduction on the same open and closed identity component. This also identifies their restricted group operations. In particular $H$ is smooth connected and of finite type. Its inclusion $i:H\hookrightarrow E$ is a closed immersion. A closed subscheme of the affine $E$ is affine by the quotient-ring description in [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Its inclusion is finite by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-finite]; since $p$ is finite, $q=p\circ i$ is finite by [lem-trf-finite-radicial-basechange].

source.place: Propositions 1.26 and 1.38, Corollary 1.39, printed pp.13,17--18; Proposition 18.6(a), printed p.388; closed immersions finite: Stacks 035C

proof.text: We now prove $q$ surjective, rather than assuming that reduction or passage to a component preserves faithful flatness. By [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates], the finitely many components $C_j$ of $E$ are translates $e_jE^\circ$ for points $e_j\in E(F)$. Set $Z=p(|E^\circ|)$. This is closed in $G$ by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-closed-map-finite-fibres], since $E^\circ$ is closed and $p$ is finite. Equivariance gives $p(|C_j|)=p(e_j)Z$. These finitely many closed translates cover $G$ because $p$ is surjective. The connected group $G$ is irreducible by [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], applied to $G$ whose identity component is all of $G$. An irreducible space cannot be a union of two proper closed subsets; induction gives the same for any finite union. Thus one translate $p(e_j)Z$ equals $G$, and translating back gives $Z=G$. Finally $H$ and $E^\circ$ have the same underlying space by step 3, so $q(|H|)=Z=G$.

source.place: Proposition 18.6(a), printed p.388, expanded using Proposition 1.34 and Corollary 1.35, printed pp.16--17; finite maps closed: Stacks 01WN

proof.text: For each $g\in G(F)$, apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-geometric-point-lift] to the finite surjective map $q$ and the geometric point $g:\operatorname{Spec}F\to G$. It produces $h\in H(F)$ with $q(h)=g$. The affine finite-type groups $H,G$ satisfy the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-affine-group-homomorphism-image], and its target $G$ is smooth by assumption. Hence this surjectivity on $F$-points implies that $F[G]\to F[H]$ is faithfully flat, exactly in the coordinate-algebra sense required by the item.

source.place: Proposition 5.47, printed pp.110--111; lifting finite geometric fibres: Stacks 02NU, 01TG and 09GU

proof.text: Compute kernels as fibre products with the identity [def-sc-group-scheme]. By the defining universal property [def-pc-fibre-product], $\ker p\simeq\ker s=\mu_n$: an element over any $F$-scheme is a pair $(1,u)$ with $s(u)=1$. The identification with the scalar subgroup is the one of [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover]. Moreover $\ker q=H\times_E\ker p$, so $\ker q\hookrightarrow\mu_n$ is the base change of the closed immersion $H\hookrightarrow E$, hence closed by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change]. This computation is on schemes, including nonreduced tests. Its coordinate algebra is a quotient of $F[z,z^{-1}]/(z^n-1)$. Since $z^{-1}=z^{n-1}$ and $z^n=1$, this algebra, and every quotient, is spanned over $F$ by $1,z,\ldots,z^{n-1}$. Thus $\ker q$ has finite-dimensional coordinate algebra. Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] with $r=1$ to the closed subgroup $\ker q\subset\mu_n\subset\mathbf G_m$. It yields $\ker q\simeq D(M)$ with $M$ finite, and exactly the group-algebra Hopf operations in the item. Together with step 5 this makes $q$ a multiplicative isogeny.

source.place: Example 5.49, printed p.111; Theorems 12.8 and 12.9(a),(c), printed pp.233--234; closed base change: Stacks 01QR

proof.text: Let $r:E\to\operatorname{SL}(V)$ be the second projection and set $\rho=r\circ i$. Both projections and $i$ are homomorphisms by steps 2--3. The fibre-product identity [def-pc-fibre-product] gives $s\circ r=a\circ p$; precomposing with $i$ gives $\overline\rho=a\circ q$. Steps 3, 5 and 6 establish every other assertion. At no point did we assume $n$ invertible in $F$; in particular the scalar kernel computation retains $\mu_n$ with its full scheme structure.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 18.22, proof p.393, with its implicit reduction justified as in Proposition 18.6(a), p.388; component-surjectivity argument expanded from Propositions 1.34 and 5.47.

Step checks: (1) For n=1, PGL=SL=1, so E=G; G is smooth, hence reduced, so H=G. (2) The matrix-cover node gives SL_r→PGL_r finite flat of rank r with scalar kernel μ_r, and PGL affine. The frames node gives the Zariski quotient by scalars; because it is representable it equals the item's fppf quotient. p is finite and surjective by base change, and E is affine and of finite type. (3) The identity-component node gives (E°)_red smooth and connected with the same space as E°, and (E°)_red=(E_red)°=H, since reduction is local and the identity on spaces. q is finite as a closed immersion composed with p. (4) Surjectivity: E has finitely many components e_jE° (no reducedness assumed), p(E°) is closed because p is finite, and G is irreducible, so one translate p(e_j)p(E°) is all of G and p(E°)=G. (5) A geometric-point lift gives H(F)→G(F) surjective, and Milne 5.47 (target G smooth) then gives faithful flatness. (6) ker q=H×_E ker p is a closed subscheme of μ_n⊂G_m, and the torus node with r=1 gives D(M) with M finite, scheme-theoretically and with no prime-to-p assumption. (7) ρ̄=a∘q comes from the defining square. Tested on n=1, trivial a (E non-reduced and disconnected), a=id (kernel μ_n with char | n), and G_m→PGL_2 via diag(t,1) (H=G_m, q(λ)=λ^{-2}, kernel μ_2, non-reduced in characteristic 2).
